issues.legal_issue: An existing provincial law may be extended retrospectively to a scheduled area by regulation.
material_facts: The area of the estates at issue in the scheduled area was outside the original territorial operation of the abolition law.
A regulation made under the Fifth Schedule extended the abolition law to that area with retrospective effect.
The proprietors challenged the regulation as exceeding the Governor’s authority because it applied an existing law rather than reproducing its provisions.
issues.conclusion: The regulation validly extended the abolition law to the scheduled area with retrospective effect.
issues.legal_principle: The court rejected the contention that a regulation under paragraph 5(2) of the Fifth Schedule could not apply an existing law retrospectively. The decision identifies no earlier case as the basis for this ruling.

predicates.challenge_to_retrospective_regulation: A party challenged the validity of a regulation extending a law to an area.
predicates.existing_law_extended_to_scheduled_area: The regulation applied an existing law to an area where that law had not previously operated.
predicates.retrospective_application_specified: The regulation specified that the extension would operate retrospectively.

issues.definition: When a challenged regulation extends an existing law to an area and specifies retrospective operation, the extension is valid.

issues.legal_issue: An estate may qualify as permanently settled even if the permanent-settlement enactment did not apply to the area in which it was situated.
material_facts: The estates were derived by subdivision from a parent zamindari situated in a scheduled district.
The permanent-settlement enactment was excluded from application to scheduled districts.
The parent zamindari had a fixed peishcush, and the proprietor’s kabuliyat conformed to the pattern of sanads and kabuliyats issued under the permanent-settlement system.
issues.conclusion: The parent zamindari was a permanently settled estate notwithstanding that the permanent-settlement enactment did not apply to the scheduled district.
issues.legal_principle: The court treated a fixed peishcush and a kabuliyat conforming to the permanent-settlement pattern as sufficient to establish permanent settlement, even if the relevant enactment did not apply. No earlier case was relied on for this ruling.

predicates.challenge_to_estate_status: A party disputed whether an estate qualified as permanently settled for purposes of a land-tenure reform.
predicates.fixed_land_revenue_assessment: The estate’s land revenue assessment had been fixed.
predicates.settlement_document_matches_permanent_se: The proprietor’s settlement document conformed to the pattern used for permanent settlements.

issues.definition: An estate is permanently settled where its assessment was fixed and its settlement document follows the permanent-settlement pattern, even if the relevant enactment did not apply to its area.

issues.legal_issue: A vesting notification may validly take over the portion of an estate within the territorial operation of the abolition law, although another portion of the same estate is outside that operation.
material_facts: The estates included land both within the ordinary territorial operation of the abolition law and within a partially excluded area where the law had not been made applicable.
An initial notification purported to vest the estates in their entirety.
Before the vesting date, the Government modified that notification to exclude the portions in the partially excluded area.
The proprietors did not obtain relief against the vesting of the portions covered by the modified notification.
issues.conclusion: The initial notification, as modified, was valid and effective to vest the portions of the estates to which the abolition law then applied.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 1(3), 2(1), and 2(3) of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, read with section 3(2) of the Madras Estates Land Act, an estate within the abolition law may be understood as the portion of a larger estate within that law’s territorial operation. The Act’s purpose of eliminating intermediaries supports taking over land within its operation rather than treating the whole estate as beyond the Act because some land lies outside its reach. The court also observed that the Act does not permit the Government to choose arbitrary portions of an estate to take over.

rule.if: challenge_to_vesting_notification and estate_part_within_lawful_territorial_scope and notification_covers_that_part and notification_excludes_area_outside_scope

predicates.challenge_to_vesting_notification: A party challenged a notification taking over an estate under a land-tenure reform law.
predicates.estate_part_within_lawful_territorial_sc: Part of the estate lay within the territorial area where the law was in force.
predicates.notification_covers_that_part: The notification provided for taking over the part of the estate within the law’s territorial operation.
predicates.notification_excludes_area_outside_scope: The notification excluded the part of the estate outside the law’s territorial operation.

issues.definition: A challenged vesting notification validly takes over the part of an estate within the law’s territorial operation when it covers that part and excludes the part outside that operation.

issues.legal_issue: A later vesting notification may validly take over the remaining portion of an estate after the law is extended to that portion, where the notifications together carry out the taking over of the estate as a whole.
material_facts: The initial notification, as modified, validly vested the portions of the estates within the abolition law’s original territorial operation.
A later regulation extended the abolition law to the remaining portions situated in the scheduled area.
The Government issued a later notification to vest those remaining portions.
The later notification was challenged on the ground that it took over only part of each estate.
issues.conclusion: The later notification was valid because, following the extension of the law, it completed the taking over of the entirety of each estate in conformity with the Act’s scheme.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3, 24, and 25 of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act reflect a scheme for taking over an estate as a unit and determining compensation for the estate as a whole. That scheme does not invalidate separate notifications which together take over the whole estate; nor does it authorize arbitrary selection of portions to take over. Once the previously excluded portion came within the Act, taking it over was necessary to complete the whole-estate vesting. No earlier case was relied on for this ruling.

rule.if: challenge_to_vesting_notification and earlier_notice_validly_vested_first_part and remaining_part_later_brought_within_law and later_notice_vests_remaining_part

predicates.challenge_to_vesting_notification: A party challenged a notification taking over an estate under a land-tenure reform law.
predicates.earlier_notice_validly_vested_first_part: An earlier notification validly took over the part of the estate then within the law’s territorial operation.
predicates.remaining_part_later_brought_within_law: A later legal change brought the previously excluded part of the estate within the law’s operation.
predicates.later_notice_vests_remaining_part: The Government issued a later notification taking over the remaining part of the estate.

issues.definition: A later vesting notification is valid where an earlier valid notice took over the first part of an estate, a subsequent legal change brought the remainder within the law, and the later notice took over that remainder.
